children.text: The year 2026 gave Vermont's reform four public tests within five months. A federal agreement ended, a governor vetoed a pricing bill, regulators cut a hospital's budget on a split vote and voters returned the governor while handing the opposing parties legislative supermajorities. The events are documented in the press, the statute and agency announcements, and together they are the best available evidence for the durability analysis of Track 1.

This lesson sets out each event in order, notes what the sources do and do not establish, and reads them against the chapter's framework. It also states what remains unknown as of late November 2026, since the 2027 legislative session has not begun.
Where an account comes from one source, the lesson says so. It takes no side on whether the policies were right.
June: The S.190 Veto

S.190 would have let the Green Mountain Care Board apply reference-based pricing to two groups: plans sold through the state's marketplace and plans offered to school employees. Its House health committee chair, Representative Alyssa Black, called it a soft opening, a dry run of the whole-market pricing that Act 68 envisions. Supporters argued that health costs drive school spending and property taxes and that marketplace plans had lost thousands of participants after enhanced federal subsidies expired.

On June 16 Governor Phil Scott vetoed it. His letter said the bill would exclude most payers from the affordability gains achieved in fiscal year 2027, and that Vermont will not solve its affordability crisis by directing savings to some payers while excluding others. He said the bill conflicted with the Board's statutory purpose, in 18 V.S.A. section 9372, of reductions across all payers, that Department of Financial Regulation analysis showed advocates' savings claims did not hold up, that the Board already has authority to reduce hospital prices and revenue, and that several rural critical access hospitals opposed the bill. He said he would advance several provisions of his own insurance package, H.585, through executive action. Board chair Owen Foster backed the bill and said there are not enough savings to go around for 2027, and the sponsor, Senator Ginny Lyons, said the governor wanted to protect insurers.
What the sources do not establish is the vote count in either chamber, whether an override was planned, or hospital association and insurer positions. This lesson did not find them.
July: The AHEAD Withdrawal

On July 24 the Agency of Human Services announced that Vermont had formally notified CMS it was withdrawing from AHEAD after new policy and operational guidance substantially reduced anticipated funding. The Green Mountain Care Board's chair supported the withdrawal, saying nothing changes for hospitals and providers because the state never began the model. The Agency's secretary said the decision would not increase costs or reduce access and pointed to the Rural Health Transformation Program, reported at $195 million a year for five years.

The event tested the durability of a federal agreement, with a clear result: it did not hold, but the state's own authority did. That is the chapter's central contrast between federal and statutory foundations.
September: The Medical Center Budget Order

On September 14 the Board voted 3 to 2 on the University of Vermont Medical Center's budget for the year beginning October 1, ordering a 4.4 percent cut to its commercial prices compared with the current year. The Board's chair and one other member dissented, while another member argued the hospital should be well placed to continue price reductions. The hospital's submitted plan was about $2.5 billion and already included a $43 million loss. Its chief executive said it could not afford another $32 million cut, that it was on track to lose $75 million this fiscal year and that the order would likely mean another $75 million loss next year. The year before, in 2025, the Board had cut $88 million from the same budget unanimously.

The event tested the Board's willingness to use its budget authority, and the split vote shows a regulator that is itself divided over pace. This lesson did not find a report that the hospital had filed a new court challenge to the September order. The book refers to the Medical Center's court challenge to the Board's enforcement, and a search found coverage saying the UVM Health Network announced in 2025 that it would appeal the earlier budget decision to the Vermont Supreme Court. The outcome of that appeal could not be confirmed here, so a reader needs to check the court's docket.
November: The Election

On November 3 Governor Scott won a sixth consecutive term, defeating Democrat and Progressive candidate Amanda Janoo, who supported publicly funded universal primary health care, by about seven points with 99 percent counted. Democrats and Progressives regained supermajorities in both chambers, and WCAX reported them with 22 Senate seats and 112 House seats. Democrat Molly Gray defeated the incumbent Republican lieutenant governor. Vermont Public reported that Scott's party would need 11 Senate seats and 51 House seats to sustain a veto, according to the Republican chair's statement as paraphrased in the article.

Senate Democrats said they wanted to use their regained power to address health care and housing. WCAX's account of the governor's reaction describes him preparing for veto showdowns. Whether health reform bills such as a successor to S.190 will be the first test is not known as of this writing, and the sources read did not report any specific bill planned for January. The legislature convenes in January, so a first test could come quickly, and organizations should have their scenario plans ready before the session starts.

body.title: Four 2026 events and what each tested

children.text: Reading the Pattern

Three observations follow. First, nothing that happened repealed or delayed the statutory core of Act 68. The mandate for reference-based pricing and the schedule for global budgets stand. Second, the contested ground was the application, which groups the pricing covers, how fast the Board moves and how much a specific hospital must cut. Third, the political configuration after November, a governor of one party and a legislature able to override him, makes the next session unusual: legislation that the governor would veto may now become law.

A fourth observation concerns timing. The events were spread across five months and each was reported separately, so a reader following only one of them would have seen a partial picture. Following all four together shows that the reform's financing, its regulation and its politics were moving at the same time.

For an organization, that third point is the main change in the risk picture. Before the election, a planner could regard a hospital-pricing bill as likely to be vetoed. After it, a planner has to treat the possibility that more aggressive legislation passes, which raises the probability of faster repricing, while the governor retains regulatory and executive tools. Track 3 turns this into scenarios.

body.message: These facts are current to late November 2026. The legislature convenes in January, courts may rule and the Board will publish further orders. Check the sources before relying on any of them for a decision, and re-check them when the new session opens.
body.title: Snapshot, not forecast

points: S.190 would have let the Board apply reference-based pricing to marketplace and school employee plans; the governor vetoed it on June 16 on fairness and authority grounds, and Act 68's mandate was unaffected.

On July 24 Vermont announced its withdrawal from AHEAD after anticipated funding was substantially reduced; the Board's chair said nothing changes for hospitals because the state never began the model.
On September 14 the Board voted 3 to 2 to order a 4.4 percent cut in the Medical Center's commercial prices, with the hospital warning of $75 million in losses.
On November 3 the governor won a sixth term by about seven points while Democrats and Progressives regained supermajorities, reported as 22 Senate and 112 House seats.
Nothing in 2026 repealed or delayed the statutory core of Act 68; the contested ground was application, pace and scope.
After the election, legislation the governor would veto may become law, raising the probability of faster repricing; the governor keeps regulatory and executive tools.
Vote counts on S.190, the status of the Medical Center's appeal and hospital and insurer positions could not be confirmed from the sources read.

body.explanation: The S.190 veto, the AHEAD withdrawal, the Board's September order and the election did not repeal or delay Act 68's reference-based pricing mandate or its global budget schedule. The contested questions were the application, pace and scope of the Board's actions.
